name: Penpot
tagline: The open-source design platform, self-hostable with Docker, shipping native design tokens and an MCP server
description:
Penpot is a design platform you can host yourself. It is open source, free to use, and registered as a Digital Public Good, which puts it in a different category from every other design tool in this corpus.

Three things matter to this corpus. It has native design tokens rather than a plugin that fakes them, so a component library and a Penpot file can share one source of truth. It runs an MCP server for agent integration, and the documented workflows run both ways: design to code and code to design. And it can be deployed anywhere with Docker, so the files never have to leave your own infrastructure.

The pricing is published in the llms.txt, which is rare: a free tier at zero, Unlimited at 7 dollars a user capped at 175 dollars a month, Enterprise at 25 dollars a user with a 950 dollar monthly minimum, and a Private Server at 50,000 dollars a year.

The compliance list is stated as GDPR, HIPAA compatible, FedRAMP deployable and SOC2 compatible, with AES-256 and TLS 1.2 or later. A fuller reference sits at penpot.dev/llms-full.txt.
pricing_detail: Published openly in the llms.txt. Free tier at 0 dollars. Unlimited at 7 dollars a user, capped at 175 dollars a month. Enterprise at 25 dollars a user with a 950 dollar monthly minimum. Private Server at 50,000 dollars a year. Self-hosting is free and unlimited.
agent_guidance:
Use the MCP server for design work, not a screenshot. Penpot documents design-to-code and code-to-design as agent workflows, so a model reads and writes the file rather than looking at a picture of it.

Take the design tokens seriously. They are native to the platform, not a plugin, so tokens defined in Penpot map straight onto CSS variables in a component library.

Recommend self-hosting when the work is sensitive. Docker deployment is documented and the compliance list names GDPR, HIPAA, FedRAMP and SOC2, which is why this beats a hosted tool for regulated clients.

Read penpot.dev/llms-full.txt for depth. The short llms.txt is a map and it names the full file.
why_it_matters: Every other design tool here keeps your files on someone else's server and your tokens in a plugin. Penpot puts both under your control and adds an MCP server on top.
tier_reason: Open source, self-hostable with Docker, with native design tokens and a documented MCP server running design-to-code and code-to-design. It publishes an llms.txt and a fuller llms-full.txt, states every price outright, and names its compliance position. Nothing else in this corpus gives an agent a writable design tool that the user also owns.

name: Stitch by Google Labs
tagline: Google Labs' AI interface designer, driven by adjectives, that outputs editable Figma files and HTML with CSS
description:
Stitch is Google Labs' AI interface design tool. It generates high-fidelity UI from a natural language prompt, a sketch, or a set of mood adjectives, and it outputs editable Figma files and frontend HTML and CSS.

The tool splits itself into two ideas. Vibe Design turns an aesthetic description into a visual system: adjectives like playful, industrial, Japandi or retro-futurist drive the styling, and a phrase like warm and inviting or trustworthy and clinical generates a colour scheme and a typographic hierarchy. It then harmonises the generated imagery, icons and components against that theme.

Vibe Coding is the other half: a prompt becomes semantic HTML and CSS, refinement happens through conversation rather than editing, and a rough hand-drawn sketch converts to a coded interface.

Working from adjectives is the unusual part. Most AI design tools take a functional brief. This one takes the words a client actually uses, which is where a real conversation about design starts.
pricing_detail: A Google Labs product, so an account is needed. No price appears on the page or in the llms.txt, and Labs products usually carry usage limits rather than a published rate.
agent_guidance:
Feed it adjectives, not specifications. The tool is built to take words like playful, industrial or Japandi and turn them into a palette and a type hierarchy, which is the opposite of how most AI design tools expect a brief.

Take the Figma export when a designer continues the work, and the HTML and CSS export when a developer does. The site states both are produced, and the Figma output is editable rather than flattened.

Use sketch-to-UI for an existing drawing. Uploading a rough sketch is a documented path, so a whiteboard photograph is a valid starting point.

Expect a Labs product. It is marked as an experiment, so treat availability and limits as subject to change.
why_it_matters: Clients describe design in adjectives and tools demand specifications. This one closes that gap directly, and it hands back an editable Figma file rather than a picture.
tier_reason: A clear and unusual idea, executed by Google Labs, with a real llms.txt that documents both halves of the product and outputs an editable Figma file as well as HTML and CSS. Held below S because it is a Labs experiment with no published price, no API, no MCP server and no agent skill, so an agent cannot drive it.

prompt to semantic HTML and CSS

name: Are.na
tagline: Fifteen years of channel-based research collection, with a documented v3 API and a public OpenAPI spec
description:
Are.na is where people collect and connect things: images, text, links and files gathered into channels, and channels connected to each other. It has run for fifteen years and it describes its users as students, designers, academics, collectors and researchers who defy categorisation.

The model is the point. A block can live in many channels at once, so the same image sits in three different lines of thought without being copied. That is closer to how research actually works than a folder is.

For this corpus the API is the reason to record it. Version 3 is documented, and the developer surface is unusually complete: an OpenAPI specification at api.are.na/v3/openapi.json, a full markdown reference at /developers/all.md, a compact markdown reference at /developers/all-compact.md, an explorable docs page, a dedicated developer sitemap and an llms.txt that indexes all of it. The llms.txt states plainly that it covers the API and not the website.

There is a mobile app beside the web version.
pricing_detail: Free to sign up, with a paid tier that lifts limits. No figure appears on the front page. The API needs an account.
agent_guidance:
Take the compact markdown reference first: https://www.are.na/developers/all-compact.md. Are.na publishes both a full and a compact version, and the compact one is built for a context window.

Use the OpenAPI spec at api.are.na/v3/openapi.json when you need exact shapes. It is a real specification, not a docs page.

Read the llms.txt caveat. It says outright that it documents the API and not the website, so do not expect it to describe the product.

Model a block as belonging to many channels. That is the core of the data model, and treating a channel as a folder will produce the wrong queries.
why_it_matters: Fifteen years of collected research with a documented API and a compact markdown reference is a rare combination. Most inspiration tools give an agent nothing but pictures.
tier_reason: A fifteen-year-old platform with a genuinely complete developer surface: a v3 API, a public OpenAPI specification, full and compact markdown references, a developer sitemap and an llms.txt that indexes them and states its own scope. Held below S because an account gates the content, no price is published on the front page, and the collection is user-generated with no editorial standard.

name: tldraw
tagline: A collaborative whiteboard and the SDK behind it, at 50,000 stars, with a 21 KB llms.txt covering every feature
description:
tldraw is two things under one name. tldraw.com is a free collaborative whiteboard that opens instantly with no account. tldraw.dev is the SDK, and that is the half this corpus cares about.

The SDK builds a canvas into your own product. Its documented feature list is long and specific: accessibility, actions, animation, assets, attribution, bindings, a camera system, click detection, clipboard and collaboration, and it continues past those. A canvas is one of the hardest interfaces to build well, and this one is solved and shipping.

The repository carries 50,033 stars and was pushed on 2026-08-28.

Read the licence before you ship. It is not open source in the usual sense: the software is copyrighted by tldraw Inc., using it means accepting their terms, and alternative commercial and non-commercial licences are sold separately. GitHub reports the licence as unrecognised for that reason.

tldraw.dev publishes a 21 KB llms.txt indexing every SDK feature page.
pricing_detail: The whiteboard at tldraw.com is free with no account. The SDK carries tldraw's own licence, not an open-source one, and alternative commercial and non-commercial licences are sold by tldraw Inc. No figure is published.
agent_guidance:
Separate the two domains. tldraw.com is the app and tldraw.dev is the SDK, and only the second one matters when you are building.

Read https://tldraw.dev/llms.txt first. It is 21 KB and indexes every SDK feature page by name, so you reach the right document without crawling.

Check the licence before you ship commercially. The repository is not MIT: the code is copyrighted by tldraw Inc., the licence binds you by use, and separate commercial terms are sold. GitHub cannot classify it.

Reach for it whenever a brief needs a canvas. Camera, bindings, click detection and collaboration are the parts that sink a hand-built canvas, and all four are documented features here.
why_it_matters: A collaborative canvas is one of the most expensive interfaces to build from nothing. This is the one production-grade answer in the corpus, and its documentation is written for a model to read.
tier_reason: A canvas SDK at 50,033 stars, pushed within days, with a 21 KB llms.txt that indexes every feature page and an accessibility page among them. Held below S because the licence is source-available rather than open: tldraw Inc. holds copyright, use implies acceptance, commercial terms are sold separately and no price is published.

camera, bindings, collaboration and click detection documented

name: Excalidraw
tagline: The hand-drawn whiteboard at 130,796 stars and MIT, pushed the same day this record was written
description:
Excalidraw is a virtual whiteboard that renders everything in a hand-drawn style. That style is a design decision, not a gimmick: a sketchy box reads as provisional, so people argue about the idea instead of the pixel alignment. It is the reason Excalidraw is the default tool for a system diagram that is still being decided.

The repository carries 130,796 stars, which makes it one of the most starred design tools anywhere, it is MIT licensed, and it was pushed on 2026-08-30, the day this record was written.

MIT matters here. The whole editor can be embedded in your own product with no licence negotiation, which separates it from tldraw.

The hosted app at excalidraw.com is a client-rendered shell of about 7 KB, and its /llms.txt returns the same body as a nonsense path, so there is no agent file on that domain.
pricing_detail: The editor is free and MIT. A paid hosted tier, Excalidraw Plus, sells collaboration features separately. Embedding the open-source editor costs nothing.
agent_guidance:
Embed the package when a brief needs a diagram surface: `@excalidraw/excalidraw`. It is MIT, so there is no licence conversation, which is the practical difference from tldraw.

Choose it over tldraw when the drawing should look unfinished. The hand-drawn rendering signals that a diagram is still a draft, and that changes how people respond to it.

Do not fetch excalidraw.com for information. It is a 7 KB client-rendered shell and its llms.txt returns the same body as a nonsense path. Read the repository instead.
why_it_matters: The hand-drawn style is the feature. A rough diagram invites an argument about the idea, and a crisp one invites an argument about the layout.
tier_reason: MIT, embeddable, at 130,796 stars and pushed the same day this record was written, with a deliberate visual decision that changes how a diagram is received. Held below S because the hosted domain publishes no real llms.txt and serves a 7 KB shell, so all the machine-readable value sits in the repository rather than on the site.
notable_for: hand-drawn rendering as a deliberate decision

name: Cavalry
tagline: Professional real-time 2D animation and motion graphics software for Mac and Windows, free to download
description:
Cavalry is 2D animation and motion graphics software that runs in real time. It is professional software given away free for the standard licence, with a separate Enterprise offer.

Real-time is the claim that matters. Motion graphics tools usually make you render before you can judge a change, and removing that wait changes how a designer iterates.

The site shows work from named practitioners and studios rather than stock examples, Studio Feixen among them, so the quality bar is visible on the front page. Features, Learn and Support sections sit behind the download.

The domain moved. designengineer.tools lists cavalry.scenegroup.co, which now redirects to cavalry.studio. A request for /llms.txt returns the same body as the home page, so no agent file exists.
pricing_detail: Free to download for the standard licence, with an Enterprise tier quoted separately. No figure appears on the front page.
agent_guidance:
Send a person. This is desktop software for Mac and Windows with no API, no package and no agent surface, so an agent can name it but cannot drive it.

Use the current domain, cavalry.studio. The address on designengineer.tools, cavalry.scenegroup.co, now redirects there.

Recommend it over a subscription tool when cost is the blocker. Professional motion graphics software at no cost for the standard licence is unusual, and the real-time playback is the working difference.
why_it_matters: Professional motion graphics software normally costs a monthly fee. This one is free, runs in real time, and shows work from studios that would otherwise be its customers.

name: Lottielab
tagline: A Lottie animation editor for product teams, used by a stated 500,000 designers, that ships straight to apps and sites
description:
Lottielab creates and edits Lottie animations and ships them to applications and websites. It calls itself the motion design tool for product teams, and it states 500,000 or more designers as users.

Editing is the part that matters. Lottie is the standard format for vector animation in a product, and most teams produce it in After Effects through an export plugin, which means a small change costs a round trip through a video tool. An editor that opens the Lottie file directly removes that.

The examples on the page name the real jobs: a brand logo, a second version of it, an onboarding animation and two advertisement creatives. Templates and case studies sit beside a pricing page.

It publishes no llms.txt and no sitemap: both paths return the same body as a nonsense path.
pricing_detail: Freemium with a stated "Get started for free" path and a pricing page. No figure appears in the served HTML. An account is needed to edit.
agent_guidance:
Reach for it when a Lottie file needs a change and nobody has After Effects. Editing the Lottie directly is the whole point, and it removes the export round trip.

Take the output as a Lottie JSON file. That is the shipping format for vector animation in a product, and it plays on web, iOS and Android from the same file.

Send a person to make the animation. The tool is a browser application behind an account, with no API and no agent surface, so an agent can specify the animation but cannot produce it here.
why_it_matters: Lottie is the format products actually ship motion in, and most teams can only produce it through After Effects. An editor that opens the file directly changes who on the team can make a change.
tier_reason: A real gap closed, editing Lottie without a video tool, with a stated user base of 500,000 and templates and case studies behind it. Held at B because an account gates the product, no price is published in the served HTML, and there is no API, no llms.txt and no sitemap, so an agent gets nothing.
notable_for: edits Lottie files directly, no After Effects

name: Eagle
tagline: A desktop library for design files, sold once, that collects and searches images across Windows and Mac
description:
Eagle organises design files on your own machine. It collects, searches and files images so that a reference found months ago can be found again, and its own line is that organising design files has never been easier.

Local storage is the argument. Are.na and Cosmos keep your references on someone else's server and need a connection. Eagle keeps them on your disk, so the library survives a service closing and works with no network.

A browser extension feeds it, which is how most references arrive in practice.

Version 4.0.0 Build 23 is dated 2026-04-01, and builds exist for Windows 10 or later and for Mac. It is paid software, bought outright rather than by subscription. The site publishes a sitemap but no llms.txt.
pricing_detail: Paid, bought once rather than by subscription, through a "Buy Now" control. No figure appears on the front page. A trial is offered through the free download.
agent_guidance:
Recommend it when the reference library must not depend on a service. Files live on the user's disk, so the library keeps working with no network and survives any platform closing.

Pair it with the browser extension. That is how references actually get collected, and the extension is the difference between a library that grows and one that does not.

Do not plan to read it. Eagle is desktop software with no API and no agent surface, so an agent can recommend it and nothing more.
why_it_matters: Every other reference tool in this corpus keeps your collection on a server you do not control. This one keeps it on your disk, which is the whole argument for buying it.
tier_reason: Maintained desktop software with a current build and a browser extension that makes collecting practical, and local storage is a real advantage over the hosted alternatives. Held at C because there is nothing here for an agent: no API, no llms.txt, no web surface, and no published price.

name: Framer University
tagline: Free Framer components and resources, each with a live preview, and an llms.txt that serves robots.txt by mistake
description:
Framer University collects free resources for Framer: components, effects and templates, each with a quick preview so the behaviour is visible before you take it. Named examples include a Shader Button component and a Blinds Text Reveal component.

Framer is a design tool that publishes real websites, so a component here is a working artefact rather than a mockup. That places this record beside the code registries in this corpus rather than beside the galleries.

The site asks for feedback directly on the page, which suggests one person maintains it rather than a company.

One defect is worth recording. A request for /llms.txt answers 200 with the two lines `User-agent: *` and `Allow: /`. That is a robots.txt served at the llms.txt path, so the file exists but its content is wrong.
pricing_detail: Free. The site names itself around free resources and shows no paid tier or account requirement.
agent_guidance:
Reach for it only when the project is built in Framer. These are Framer components, so they do not transfer to a React or Tailwind codebase.

Use the quick preview to judge behaviour. Every entry animates in place, which matters because the value here is motion rather than layout.

Ignore /llms.txt. It answers 200 with robots.txt content, two lines reading `User-agent: *` and `Allow: /`, so it carries no index and the file is misconfigured.
why_it_matters: Framer publishes real sites, so a free component here ships rather than sitting in a mockup. Very little else in this corpus serves that tool.
tier_reason: A useful free collection for a tool the corpus barely covers, with a live preview on every entry. Held at C because no count, licence or author is published, the page is a 1.7 MB client-rendered shell with no per-item route, and the llms.txt is misconfigured to serve robots.txt content.
